full_judgment:
Bangladesh Shilpa Bank after liberation of Bangladesh filed Miscellaneous Case No.70 of 1980 under Article 33 of the Bangladesh Shilpa Bank Order, 1972 and got an order of add interim attachment of the property of the Company mortgaged with the Bangladesh Shilpa Bank. The said case was subsequently re-numbered as Miscellaneous Case No.53 of 1985. Bangladesh Shilpa Bank, however, ultimately withdrew the said Miscellaneous case and took forcible possession of the Mill of the company and compelled the respondent to write some letters and to sign an agreement dated 13.10.86 admit-ting liability of his indebtedness to the Bank and also obtained some post-dated cheques and a pay order from the said respondent by coercive method and undue influence. Thereafter the company filed Title Suit No.49 of 1987 in the Court of 3rd Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for a declaration that the said agreement was void and for refund of money illegally realised from the Company. The Bank is its-turn filed a criminal case against respondent Mirza Ali Ashraf in connection with the post-dated cheques. Respondent No.1 appeared in court and obtained bail and ultimately he was discharged on 4.7.87. Thereafter respondent No.1 was arrested on 24.2.87 and was taken to Dhaka Central Jail and was served with an order of detention under Section 3(1)(a) of the Special Powers Act for three months. The grounds of detention were served on 9.3.87. Subsequent there to the period of detention was extended for further three months. While respondent No.1 was in detention respondent No.3 Dr. Mahiuddin Khan Alamgir, the then Managing Director of the Bangladesh Shilpa Bank, constantly there attended the wife and brother of Mirza Ali Ashraf who were Directors of the Company to come to terms. The Bank also filed a criminal case against respondent No.1 and other Directors of the Company on 8.6.87 under Section 60(1)(a) of the Special Powers Act. In view of the constant threats respondent No. 1 and other Directors transferred all their shares in favour of the party nominated by the said Managing Director and handed over pos-session of the same on 6.7.87. Thereafter respondent Mirza Ali Ashraf was released from custody. The case of respondent No.1 that ;le was detained with a malafide motive to get his property transferred to the nominees of the Bank at the instance of the said Bank Officers and not for any purpose or any ground under the Special Powers Act. Hence, after release from detention respondent No.1 filed this writ petition for a declaration that the order of detention was without any lawful authority and of no legal effect. 

 6. The writ petition that was filed before the High Court Division by respondent No.1 is not in the nature of a petition of habeas corpus as contemplated under Article 102(2) (b) (i) of the Constitution for the release of a person in custody. After the release of the detenu the writ petition was filed by the detenu himself seeking for a declaration that the action taken by the petitioner and respondent Nos. 2-4 are without lawful authority and of no legal effect. The learned Judges of the High Court Division on consideration of the grounds of detention served on the detenu found that the grounds relate to non-payment of loan taken by the company of which respondent No.1 was the Managing Director. According to the learned Judges the main object of detention appeared to be realisation of the loan which was not contemplated under section 3 of the Special Powers Act and consequently the learned Judges found no nexus between the order of detention and the grounds served. The learned Judges found that the order of detention was passed without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect. The learned Judges further found that respondent No.1 was released after executing some papers transferring his Mill and after doing certain other acts. The learned Judges held that the purported action of detaining respondent No.1 being not authorised by law respondent No.1 was entitled to such a declaration under Article 102(2) (a) (ii) of the Constitution. We also find that in the facts and circum-stances of the case, respondent No.1 is entitled to such a declaration as has been found by the learned Judges of the High Court Division.
